title: Did time have a beginning?
teaches: What Einstein's theory says about the first moment, why it predicts its own failure there, and what is well tested about the Big Bang and what isn't

blocks.text: Run the expansion of the universe backwards, as *Everything is running away* did, and the galaxies crowd together. Further back, the universe was the hot, dense glowing gas of *Why is the night sky dark?*, and before that it was hotter and denser still. How far back does that go? Was there a first moment?

Georges Lemaître, the Belgian priest who first worked out the expansion, was also the first to follow it all the way back. In 1931 he proposed that the universe began as a single “primeval atom”, a kind of enormous nucleus holding all the matter there is, which broke up and expanded on a day without a yesterday. Many physicists disliked it. A beginning of the universe sounded far too much like the first chapter of Genesis, and coming from a priest that made them doubly suspicious. Lemaître himself insisted the science and his religion had nothing to do with each other, and when Pope Pius XII declared in 1951 that science had confirmed the Creation, Lemaître quietly persuaded him to stop saying so.

Fred Hoyle's Steady State was in part a way to avoid a beginning: a universe that had always existed, and always looked the same. By 1965 the afterglow had settled that the universe really had been hot and dense. But a hot, dense past is not the same as a first moment. Perhaps the universe had shrunk to some small size and bounced, or perhaps the crowding stopped short of anything infinite. Most physicists assumed that, somehow, it did.

parts.title: A theorem about the end of stars

blocks.text: The surprise came from black holes. Oppenheimer and Snyder's 1939 calculation (*Dark stars*) showed a collapsing star crushed to a point of infinite density, a singularity, at its centre. But they had assumed a perfectly round, perfectly smooth star. Real stars aren't smooth, and it seemed possible that any small lumpiness would make the infalling matter miss the centre and swirl back out, so that real collapses never produced a singularity at all.

In 1965 the British mathematician Roger Penrose proved otherwise. Using only general relativity and the reasonable assumption that energy is never negative, he showed that once a collapsing star has passed a certain point, a singularity must form, lumpy or not. His method didn't need anything to be smooth; it used the geometry of light cones, the picture from *Muons that live too long*, and showed that the cones tip over inward and every path ends.

A young research student at Cambridge, Stephen Hawking, saw what that meant. The expanding universe, run backwards, is like a collapsing star played in reverse. If Penrose's argument worked for a star falling in, a version of it should work for a universe coming out. In 1970 Hawking and Penrose published a theorem together: if general relativity is right, and the universe contains about as much matter as we see, then it must have begun in a singularity. Time itself, in Einstein's theory, has a beginning.

blocks.text: Here is the twist, and it is the honest end of the trunk. A singularity is a place where the quantities in a theory become infinite: infinite density, infinite temperature, infinite curvature of space and time. Physicists take infinities as a theory's way of saying it has been pushed beyond what it can describe. So the Hawking–Penrose theorem says two things in the same breath. General relativity predicts that the universe had a beginning. And general relativity predicts that at that beginning, general relativity itself fails.

What takes over? Close enough to the first moment, everything we can now see was crowded into a space smaller than an atom, and the small is the territory of quantum physics: the rules of atoms, the energy ladders of *A schoolteacher's number puzzle* and the light packets of *Why are there no green stars?* Einstein's gravity and the rules of atoms each work superbly on their own ground, but where both matter at once they disagree. A theory joining the two is called **quantum gravity**, and nobody has one that works. Hawking spent much of his later life on the question, and proposed with James Hartle, in what they called the **no-boundary** idea, that the universe might have no edge in time at all, in the way the Earth's surface has no edge at the North Pole. It is an elegant idea and, like the other proposals, untested speculation.

parts.title: What we know, and what we don't

blocks.text: Strip away the parts nobody can test and a great deal is left. From about a second after the start, the hot Big Bang is as well tested as anything in science. It predicted how much helium and deuterium the first minutes would make, and those amounts are what we find in the oldest gas. It predicted the afterglow, and COBE found its curve perfect to one part in ten thousand. It explains the dark night, the expansion and the redshifts, and the ages of the oldest stars fit inside it. About the first moment itself, the theory we have predicts its own failure, and the theory we need doesn't exist yet. The branch on cosmic beginnings goes as far as anyone can, and labels the speculation as it goes.

blocks.text: Go back to the beginning of this course: Eratosthenes in Egypt, around 240 BC, measuring two shadows and working out the size of the Earth. Everything since has been the same trick: take a small, careful measurement, add a law of nature you trust, and see how far it reaches. Shadows gave the Earth's size; the Moon's fall gave the law of gravity; a wobble of starlight gave the distance to a star; the dark lines in sunlight gave the stuff of the stars; Leavitt's flickering stars opened the road to the size of the universe; a hiss in a horn antenna gave its hot past. We don't know whether time had a beginning. But a species that started with sticks in the sand has worked out what happened in the universe's first three minutes, and that it is 13.8 billion years old. That is not a bad start.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the beginning
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

choices: A collapsing star past a certain point must form a singularity, even if it isn't perfectly smooth
items.why: Using only general relativity and light cones, he showed lumpiness can't save a collapsing star from a singularity.

choices: Run backwards, the expanding universe is like a collapse, so it too must begin in a singularity, if general relativity holds
That the universe has no beginning
items.why: The Hawking–Penrose theorem of 1970 applies the same reasoning to the universe as a whole.

items.ask: Why don't physicists take the singularity at time zero as a real point of infinite density?
choices: Infinities mean the theory has gone beyond what it can describe
Infinite density has been measured to be impossible
items.why: At that moment quantum effects must matter, and general relativity leaves them out. A theory of quantum gravity is needed.

items.ask: Which part of the Big Bang story is well tested?
choices: The hot, dense early universe from about a second on: helium, deuterium, the afterglow
What came before the Big Bang
items.why: The amounts of light elements and the afterglow's perfect glow curve match predictions. Time zero is beyond our theories.

items.ask: Hawking and Hartle's “no-boundary” idea is best described as…
items.why: It is one proposal for how quantum gravity might handle the first moment. Nothing yet tests it.

summary: **Run the expansion back and everything crowds together.** Lemaître's 1931 primeval atom was the first picture of a beginning.
**Penrose, 1965.** A collapsing star past a certain point must form a singularity, smooth or not.
**Hawking and Penrose, 1970.** If general relativity holds, the universe began in a singularity.
**The theory predicts its own failure.** At the singularity general relativity breaks down; quantum gravity, which nobody has yet, is needed.
**The hot Big Bang is well tested.** From about a second on: helium, deuterium, the afterglow, the expansion.
**Whether time had a beginning is still open.** Proposals like Hawking and Hartle's no-boundary idea are speculation.
